5 money rules my wife and I follow as a couple aged 45 with two kids.

1. We don’t spend money to look rich. 

We spend to become wealthy and gain freedom of our time.

So, there’s no car. It’s rented. 
We own the house we live in, no other real estate.

No spending on brands. No spending just to show off to people.

2. We spend extravagantly on high-quality food.

We know that what goes into our body is ultimately the biggest wealth we have, and unfortunately, healthy food is not cheap.

3. We spend on experiences more than things.

Things give you happiness once, and they have no end.

You remember experiences, and they make you a better person. 
You grow as a person.

We travelled 116 days last year!

4. We invest before spending.

As soon as our salary comes, the largest amount is invested.

The remaining amount is used for expenses.

We are recording this on the 30th. 
₹9,000 and ₹600 left in our bank accounts. 
Everything else is invested.

5. No budget for books and learning.

No amount of money spent is enough.

Ruchi is learning pottery, watercolor painting, and tennis.

Our kids also go to many classes.

These are our rules. 
They may not apply to you, but having your own rules is important in life.

Before you say yes to marriage, check these 5 things.

1. Why are you getting married? Is it for the sake of society? Is it for the sake of your parents? Is it for your own good?

2. How do you handle fights with your partner? Because fights will continue. If you handle them properly, then relationships will progress.

3. Do you have an alignment on money and responsibility? How will you spend money? How will you share responsibilities?

4. Do you have space for your own personality? You can make friends without involving their friends. You can live your own life without depending on them.

5. How will you spend your life after marriage? What are the expectations from your family? How will your daily routines be? What will be your living arrangements? What have you thought about your children?

This is an important decision. Don't take it in a hurry.

Clear any interview with this 5-day challenge.

On Day 1 - prepare your 90-second introduction.

You have to focus on 4 things:
What are you doing right now?
What relevant experience do you have?
What are the things you are really good at?
And what do you want to do next?

Day 2 - design your proof.

This is all the evidence you can show a recruiter if they need any proof - proof of your work, internships, experience, and knowledge too.

Day 3 - practice stress interviews.

Pick your most powerful, strongest story or strength. Put it into ChatGPT and tell it to ask you follow-up stress questions. Answer them without preparing.

Day 4 - learn to answer a question whose answer you don’t know.

Upload your resume to ChatGPT and ask it to pose 30 questions that are not obvious, very difficult, and almost out of syllabus, and try to answer all of them.

Day 5 - do a 20-minute mock interview.

Activate ChatGPT voice and tell it your full context, and then say, “Take an interview in English.”

This 5-day training and preparation can help you prepare for every interview.

If a friend or relative asks you for money, how do you handle it without making things awkward?

These 5 rules can help.

1/ Never lend more than you are comfortable losing.

2/ If you can give the money, don’t treat it as a loan. 
Tell yourself, “If I get it back, that’s great, but I assume this money won’t come back.”

3/ If you cannot lend the money, say so directly. 
If you beat around the bush, it will make things awkward.

4/ For large amounts, always put it in writing.

5/ Never lend money again to someone who hasn’t returned it the first time.

A girl went to college and forgot her parents. 
After many days, she wrote them a letter:

“Maa, Papa, before you read this, I want you to sit down. I wanted to tell you that as soon as I went to college, my room caught fire. 

I had to jump out of my window to save my life. 

God bless the boy who came running and saved my life. 
He would come to see me in the hospital. 
We became friends and I don’t know when that friendship turned into love. 

Now, we are married. 
There was no hurry, but my pregnancy is visible now. 
And I didn’t want it to show at the wedding.

Maa, Papa, please listen carefully. 

There was no fire, I don’t have a boyfriend, I am not pregnant, and whatever I said was not true. 

I just failed all my exams.”

Now, see how quickly this letter changed. 
But why? 

Because perspective is everything. 

If the daughter straight away told them that she failed, then that wouldn’t have worked. 

But suddenly, seeing all these things, the parents would have said, “You just failed. 
No problem, work harder next time.” 

Perspective changes everything!

Who said in India people only pay for music concerts and entertainment?

Look at the biggest convention center of the country jam packed with thousands of people, who are there for growth.

India is changing and India wants to grow🫡 

Post 1: Look at the face of this kid on the stage who is living a dream he saw at the age of 19 with no money, no influence and no fancy degree, to deliver a speech in front of fully sold out stadium. 🫣

Post 2: My parents saw me live at a conference for the first time, this proud look on their face is the reason why I am happy crying rn❤️

Post 3: Me looking at all of you, and thanking every god in the world. What have I done right to deserve an audience like yours? 🤍🥺

At age 16, I used to go to English classes to learn how to speak English fluently and while sitting in the tuition centre I used to write random dreams at the back of my notebook. 😂 

I had no talent, no background, was not from a big city, did not have good grades to make it to IIT / IIM, and wasn’t even able to speak in English properly but I used to believe that I had ‘shaka-laka boom boom magic) 😂 

29th July 2013 - I wrote in my dairy that I will be on the cover of Forbes magazine, (I and my sisters laughed at this crazy dream)

Age 26 - I made it to Forbes cover and Forbes 30 under 30.😭😭

And at this moment, the teenager in me is screaming at the top of his lungs that 'we made it.'

And today, the big dream has finally hit this boy from a small city -Indore.

This would have never been possible without your love and belief in me.

Truth be told, I started my entrepreneurship journey when I was 16 solely because I wanted to achieve this🤫

But along the line, I have fallen in love with the process of educating and helping 100s and 1000s of people.🥺

Coming from a humble family and city, having big dreams was considered a 'luxury.' But today as I get acknowledged for fulfilling mine, it isn't just me who wins.

This is a win for everyone who doubts themselves for not being talented enough, 
not being rich enough, not being from the big city, not being an IIM/IIT graduate & still continue to believe in their dreams. 

it’s a win for all of them, all of us.❤️

Now that we have this baby home, I am ready to go back to basics and fulfil my duty of building the nation, one day at a time.

P.S. Thank you all from the deepest corner of my heart, each of you that has supported me has a special place in my heart. 😭

Onam Ashamsakal! Celebrating Onam with my Kerala team is always my favourite kind of masterclass.

First, mascaras! I’d been puzzled by how much they sell here when you rarely see them on their beautiful kohl-rimmed eyes. Turns out it’s got nothing to do with lashes - Kerala women have been using these to cover the greys in their gorgeous thick, wavy hair. Talk about jugaad :)

Then, Thrissur. I first heard of the town back in 2001, when my Electrical Engineering batch at IIT Madras had all of 3 girls in a class of 120. One of them was from Thrissur, from a conservative Muslim family for whom simple things I took for granted, like being sent away to a hostel, were quite a big deal. Fast forward to today: at just 3 lakh people, Thrissur ranks 16th among Indian cities by GDP contribution. And you can feel it in the infrastructure, even in the air conditioning at the smallest of beauty stores.

And it’s not just Thrissur. Met colleagues from Kottayam, Palakkad, Kannur pulling the same store sales as some metros - many of them holding up their families as the sole breadwinners. 

Kerala makes it palpable what a 92% female literacy rate does for a place and reminds you that empowering stories around women aren’t being written only in the big metros 💛

latestIgtvVideos.caption:
Long Post Alert! Most EPIC Kolkata Itinerary that you will find #AD This is my #Indiagenous journey to Kolkata with @agoda to explore India through fresh eyes. I found some great value deals with Agoda's GoLocal campaign for flights and from 80,000 + properties to choose from across India I set my heart at Kolkata and booked ITC Sonar @itcroyalbengal  because the pics looked gorgeous and it was super centrally located. 

Day 1
1) Checked into the hotel and I had prebooked (12 hours in advence) a Bengali thali experience at the hotel. Some local favs are available anyway on the menu. You can also opt to visit Sonar Tori for a lavish Bengali feast. 
2) Fruit Cake at Nahoum's Bakery (100+ years now) in New Market.
3) Pick some Bandel Cheese from S Panja at New Market.
4) Head to UP Bihar for B**f Bhuna or Mutton/B**f Kathi Roll
5) Stroll around and shop for spices
6) Catch a kaali peeli to Blue Poppy Thakali at Middleton Road.

Day 2 
1) Get noods and Shingara Chow for b'fast at Kim Li 
2) Do a misthi trail - 
a) Get a mixed Sandesh box at Girish Chandra Dey & Nakur Chandra Nandy in Hedua.
b) Madhuporko and Roshogulla at Chittaranjan Mistanna Bhandar in Shyam Bazaar
c) Classic mithai making at Makhan Lal & sons in Natun Bazaar.
3) Kolkata Biryani at Zam Zam Restaurant in Entally.
4) Go for a walk at Prinsep Ghat. Get Ghoti Gorom from a local vendor.
5) Get a beer at the iconic Broadway Hotel.
6) Dive into Kabiraji cutlets at Mitra Cafe, Shobha Bazaar.
7) Night walk at Park St. and Kathi Rolls at Kusum.

Day 3
1) Morning drive on Howrah Bridge and around.
2) Chai and Malai Toast at Kona Dukaan at stock exchange.
3) Visit the iconic Victoria Memorial Park.
4) Lemon Tarts and Chicken Envelope at Kookie Jar
5) Jhalmuri & Phuchka at Vardaan Market.
6) Blueberry Coffee at Roastery coffee house
7) Indo chinese Dinner at Golden Joy, Tangra

This Indiagenous trip was incredible and now I’m probably a part bong with my eating and sleeping escapades. Kolkata truly is not just a city, it's an emotion. I will be back because my heart wants more of this city. I’d just like to say Ashi, Kolkata. Ami Tomake Bhalobhashi.

My US visa was first rejected in June, 2011. Why? Because I was unmarried or jobless, I guess. My dream was to travel to LA with the last batch of my savings to try my luck at the food network to pursue my dream of being a chef in the food content industry! I wanted to merge my passion for cooking and acting, together. I was shattered when this last attempt to live my dream was rejected (after having already faced multiple rejections in Mumbai in 2010).

After a month out of nowhere I got a call from 'FoodFood' tv channel to come for a life changing audition, later I was told it was through an email I had dropped back in the year 2010 when I was struggling to be in Mumbai. After my audition I was shortlisted to be on Mahachallenge. Life took a turn on that show, I went on to win it and I also met my idol Chef Sanjeev Kapoor.

Then 9 months later - March, 2012 - I was invited to the US to represent Indian cuisine and a young interviewer at the Visa consulate asked "Why was your Visa rejected, I can't understand, also with a polite smile he told me that I didn't have to carry amy newspaper clippings to prove a point. Please teach me more about Indian food" he said. I wish I could explain to him that life had happened to me. If I had gone earlier to the US, who knows I might have struggled all my life. My rejection made me who I am today. This is Arbhi tuk canape that I made for a demo in New York to showcase how beautiful Indian cuisine is. I would not change a single thing about this journey because if you dare to dream, life will happen to you.

Simple moong dal, slowly cooked till creamy… and then Moradabad goes to town on it with butter, bhuna jeera, mirchi, pyaaz, nimbu, chutney, papdi and chaat masala.

The dal is humble. The toppings are where the personality begins.

And that malai-like layer that forms while the dal rests? Please don’t throw it away. That’s gold. 🤌 My grandfather would specially ask for that.

My mornings don’t change much. Same quiet 30 minutes before anyone needs anything from me. Same handful of decisions I don’t have to think about — what I eat, when I move, when the laptop opens and when it shuts. None of it photographs well. None of it would make an interesting reel on its own.

But here’s what I’ve noticed — the days that go well aren’t the days something exciting happens. They’re the days the boring stuff already happened, so I have the bandwidth left for whatever actually needs my full attention. A predictable routine isn’t the opposite of ambition. It’s what makes ambition sustainable past the first few months of adrenaline. 
  If your day feels chaotic, the fix probably isn’t a better morning routine video. It’s picking a handful of boring decisions and making them non-negotiable, so your energy stops leaking out through a hundred small choices you didn’t need to make in the first place.

Discipline isn’t dramatic. It’s just consistent. And consistent, it turns out, is the closest thing to a cheat code any of us actually get.
